extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, and judges handling design-patent IPRs and appeals
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and tests used to evaluate anticipation and obviousness of design patents in IPRs and on Federal Circuit review, including the ordinary-observer test, Rosen/Durling two-step obviousness framework, standing, burdens, and standards of appellate review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary observer test (Gorham)
rubrics_metrics.description: "If, in the eye of an ordinary observer, giving such attention as a purchaser usually gives, two designs are substantially the same, if the resemblance is such as to deceive such an observer, inducing him to purchase one supposing it to be the other." (Gorham Co. v. White)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the perspective of an ordinary purchaser giving the attention they usually give; focus on whether resemblance would deceive that observer into buying one thinking it is the other. Applied both for infringement and for anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the ordinary observer for component-part designs
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary observer for a design patent directed to a component (e.g., a vehicle front fender) may be the purchaser of that component or others sufficiently interested in that component (e.g., repair professionals, parts-store employees), not necessarily purchasers of the assembled product (whole vehicle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the market for the part, testimony identifying who buys/installs the part, and prior case law (Arminak, Keystone) recognizing ordinary observers can be component purchasers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal-use lifetime visibility of design features
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary-observer analysis looks to features visible in the 'normal use' lifetime of the accused product — 'from the completion of manufacture or assembly until the ultimate destruction, loss, or disappearance of the article.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include features visible during repair and replacement phases; 'normal use' can encompass multiple lifecycle phases (sale, repair, replacement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation standard for design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A design is anticipated if, in the eye of the ordinary observer giving ordinary purchaser attention, the prior design creates substantially the same overall visual impression so as to deceive the ordinary observer into purchasing one supposing it to be the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation is a question of fact reviewed for substantial evidence; Board must compare designs as a whole and identify whether key differences change the overall appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rosen/Durling two-step test for design-patent obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Durling outlines a two-step analysis for design obviousness: (1) identify a primary (Rosen) reference whose design characteristics are 'basically the same' as the claimed design by discerning the visual impression of the design as a whole; (2) if a satisfactory primary reference exists, determine whether an ordinary designer would have modified the primary reference, using secondary references, to create a design with the same overall visual appearance as the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step one is a threshold: without a Rosen reference that is basically the same, the obviousness inquiry ends. Step two examines whether the modifications are suggested and would preserve the overall visual impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rosen primary-reference requirement ('basically the same')
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be 'a reference, a something in existence, the design characteristics of which are basically the same as the claimed design' to support a holding of obviousness (Rosen / citing Jennings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the mandatory starting point under Durling—courts look for a single reference that creates essentially the same visual impression as the claimed design; failure to identify such a reference is dispositive under precedent applied by the Board and this Court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durling 'so related' requirement for secondary references
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary references considered to modify the Rosen/primary reference must be 'so related [to the primary reference] that the appearance of certain ornamental features in one would suggest the application of those features to the other.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents arbitrary cherry-picking of features across unrelated designs; secondary references must be meaningfully related such that combining their ornamental features with the primary reference would be a natural/design-sense step for an ordinary designer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition against improper combination (Jennings principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: One must start with 'something in existence—not with something that might be brought into existence by selecting individual features from prior art and combining them' (Jennings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness analysis should not permit invention-by-aggregation of unrelated ornamental features that fundamentally change the overall visual impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivided first-step analysis (visual-impression articulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To assess whether a Rosen reference exists, a tribunal must (1) discern the correct visual impression created by the patented design as a whole; and (2) determine whether there is a single reference that creates 'basically the same' visual impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challengers should articulate the claimed design's overall visual impression and identify how a reference matches it; the Board may identify specific element differences (e.g., wheel-arch shape, door cut line, protrusion, sculpting, creases, inflection/concavity lines) to explain why impressions differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof in PTAB IPRs
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner in an inter partes review must prove unpatentability (anticipation or obviousness) by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to meet the preponderance standard means the Board should find the challenged claims patentable over the cited prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of appellate review
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal conclusions (e.g., ultimate determinations of law) are reviewed de novo; factual findings are reviewed for substantial evidence. Anticipation is a question of fact (substantial-evidence review); the ultimate determination of obviousness is reviewed de novo with underlying facts for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate decision will sustain the Board where a reasonable mind could accept the evidence as adequate to support the conclusion; see Campbell Soup, Int'l Seaway, Consol. Edison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial evidence explained
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantial evidence is 'such relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmance depends on whether the Board's findings are supported by evidence that a reasonable mind would accept; appellate courts do not reweigh credibility where conflicting conclusions reasonably arise from the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing to appeal (injury-in-fact for patent disputes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standing requires an injury in fact that is concrete and particularized and actual or imminent, not conjectural; a party currently engaged in conduct creating a substantial risk of infringement may have standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For standing in appeals from PTAB decisions, representations in the opening brief asserting current conduct creating substantial risk of infringement may be accepted for purposes of evaluating standing (Amerigen); evidence such as cease-and-desist letters or business of selling accused parts supports standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction approach for design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Design claims are best represented by illustrations/drawings and the correct visual impression created by the design as a whole; articulating that visual impression is central to construction for obviousness/anticipation analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and the Board often require challengers to state the overall visual impression they contend the claimed design embodies; misarticulation can be a basis for rejecting an obviousness challenge (though the appropriateness of making such misarticulation dispositive is debated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of lifecycle/market context in ordinary-observer analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Who the ordinary observer is and which features matter depend on market context (e.g., part-sellers, repair professionals) and the product lifecycle (sales, repair, replacement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of the market for individual parts and purchaser behavior (e.g., replacement fender buyers vs whole-vehicle purchasers) informs ordinary-observer identity and what aspects of appearance matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to agency credibility and factfinding
rubrics_metrics.description: Where two different, inconsistent conclusions may reasonably be drawn from the evidence, an agency's decision to favor one conclusion over the other must be sustained upon review for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts will not substitute their own credibility assessments for the Board's when reasonable inferences support the Board's findings (citing In re Jolley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural preservation/forfeiture of issues on appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: An appellate court ordinarily will not consider issues not raised before the lower tribunal; the phrasing need not be exact so long as the lower tribunal was 'fairly put on notice as to the substance of the issue.' Forfeiture may be excused in narrow circumstances (e.g., pure question of law, miscarriage of justice, significant questions of general impact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should raise legal challenges clearly to the PTAB to preserve them on appeal; appellate panels have discretion whether to address forfeited issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-vs-utility distinction in obviousness considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Although 35 U.S.C. § 103 applies to all patents, design patents protect ornamentation and are evaluated on overall appearance, artistry, and style, whereas utility patents implicate function, unexpected properties, and utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some aspects of KSR's rejection of rigid combination rules for utility patents may have limited applicability to design patents; courts may treat design-obviousness analysis differently given the ornamental focus.
